Municipal ordinance regulating and licensing personal-loan (money-lending) businesses; not a lodging- or boarding-house regulation.
Cotenancy title dispute over partitioned farmland and mineral leases decided on adverse possession/notice grounds; residences on the tracts are incidental facts, not a letting issue.

Negligence/proximate-cause suit over a fatal gas explosion in a rented tourist-court cabin; the letting arrangement is incidental background and the court never characterizes it, so it does not bear on letting doctrine despite the tourist-court setting.

Venue-statute case on whether a traveling businessman established a second 'residence' by renting a hotel room and later a room in a private residence; concerns domicile/venue doctrine, not the legal character or regulation of the letting itself.

holding_summary: The court invalidated a city ordinance rezoning a single tract from single-family residential use to apartment-house use, holding it unjustifiable 'spot zoning' beyond the city's police power because there had been no substantial change in neighborhood conditions since the original zoning. In doing so it approvingly quoted authority describing apartment houses as detrimental to residential districts and 'near nuisances.'

quotes.text: Under these circumstances, apartment houses, which in a different environment would be not only entirely unobjectionable but highly desirable, come very near to being nuisances.
the enactment of the amendatory ordinance was not within the scope of the police power of the City, and that the same is unconstitutional and void.

notes: The basic zoning ordinance (unchallenged here) groups 'Boarding or Lodging Houses' with apartment houses as a distinct, more-restricted use class kept out of single-family districts -- period regulatory evidence that multi-occupant paying arrangements were treated as quasi-commercial intrusions in residential zones. characterization left null: the court adjudicates zoning validity/police-power procedure, not the legal character (lease/license/lodging) of any specific letting arrangement. duration_of_occupancy unclear because the case concerns proposed apartment construction, not an actual tenancy.
Premises-liability suit over a customer's fall in a drugstore/garage passageway (invitee-status doctrine); no letting or lodging issue.
Statute-of-frauds dispute over an oral one-year employment/bonus contract; unrelated to residential letting.

Timberland title dispute turning on limitation and mutuality of estoppel between prior-judgment privies; no letting or lodging issue.

holding_summary: The court construed Article 4592, under which a hotel, apartment hotel, or boarding-house keeper may limit liability for a guest's lost valuables to $50 by maintaining a safe and posting the statutory notice on the guest's sleeping-room door. It held that posting the notice inside the bathroom door within the suite, rather than on the sleeping-room door itself, did not satisfy the statute. Because the hotel had not complied, its liability for the guests' stolen jewelry was to be determined under ordinary negligence principles rather than the statutory cap.

quotes.text: Any hotel, apartment hotel or boarding house keeper, who constantly has in his hotel, apartment hotel or boarding house a metal safe or vault in good order and fit for the custody of money, jewelry, articles of gold or silver manufacture, precious stones, personal ornaments, or documents of any kind, and who keeps on the doors of the sleeping rooms used by guests suitable locks or bolts and proper fastening on the transom and window of said room, shall not be liable for the loss or injury suffered by any guest on account of the loss of said valuables in excess of the sum of fifty dollars

It is evident that the Legislature enacted this law for the benefit of the hotel keepers in this state, and to relieve them from burdens imposed by • the common law in case of loss of property by guests.

We think that the Article requires that such printed copy be posted on the door of .the sleeping room' used by the guest, on which the hotel is required to keep a suitable lock or bolt. Posting the copy of Article 4592 on the bath room door, as was done in this case, was not a compliance with such Article.

notes: polarity marked favorable because the statute is legislature-granted protection treating hotel/boarding-house keeping as a recognized, protected trade; it is a liability-limitation statute rather than a right-to-let holding, so the favorable/adverse fit is imperfect. duration_of_occupancy set to 'months' because the injured guests had resided at the hotel continuously since September 1942 through trial.
